review_basis: Visually inspected all 29 original public/course-visuals/aif-course/module-08 numbered WebP images individually in order. Narration rewritten following exact diagram arrows, visible text/examples, numeric values, callouts, and exam comparisons, with product lifecycle caveats.

scenes.title: Amazon Rekognition
scenes.narration: At top left choose a photo or supported video source, then follow the arrow into Amazon Rekognition. The center-right capability panel lists three kinds of output: labels for objects and scenes, visible text detected in an image, and separate face analysis or comparison features. These outputs are suggestions for application logic, not guaranteed truths. The worked shelf photo below shows a Special Offer sign and chips, cereal and granola packages. The illustrative results include object labels such as chips and cereal and detected words such as Special Offer and Granola. An application can use those findings to review store shelves. The bottom-right comparison is a critical exam distinction: Rekognition analyzes general image and video content, whereas Textract is optimized for text, form fields and tables in scanned documents. Face detections or similarities should not be treated as proof of identity. Ask whether the goal is understanding a visual scene or extracting structured fields from a document.

scenes.title: Amazon Rekognition – Custom Labels
scenes.narration: Look at the company logo examples at top left: a leaf symbol appears on packaging, a mug and bags. Human labelers mark examples such as logo present and logo absent, and the labeled images are stored in Amazon S3. Follow the arrow to Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels, where the team trains a model, evaluates its performance and deploys it for new photographs. In the next panel a new shelf photo has a bright box around packaging labeled logo present. The final merchandising review box uses this detection to decide whether a company product is displayed appropriately. The lower worked example repeats the training dataset, model and fresh shelf image flow. The comparison panel tells you why a predefined generic image label is different from a brand-specific custom label. A generic model may find a bottle or a chair, but recognizing a particular brand logo requires labeled training data. A confidence score and a good-looking example do not guarantee accuracy across lighting and camera angles.

scenes.title: Amazon Rekognition – Content Moderation
scenes.narration: This slide begins with a user-uploaded social media image, which goes to Rekognition DetectModerationLabels. The next box lists illustrative confidence values, including 93 percent for an explicit-content label, 21 percent for violence, 8 percent for drugs and 5 percent for hate symbols. These are example outputs, not values that will occur for every image. The application policy box then defines thresholds and chooses an action. The three rightmost options are allow, queue for human review, or block. They are application decisions, not automatic actions forced by Rekognition. The dotted middle lane describes an optional custom moderation adapter trained from labeled images. The bottom worked example applies the same process to another set of illustrative scores, including an 87 percent label that crosses a chosen review threshold. The key distinction is confidence versus policy. Different organizations may apply different thresholds, and uncertain content may need human judgment.

scenes.title: Content moderation with human review
scenes.narration: Follow the top architecture from a user asking an image chatbot to create a mountain landscape. The application obtains a candidate image from an image model, then calls Amazon Rekognition DetectModerationLabels. The diamond-shaped application policy gate decides whether the image is acceptable. The green route goes directly to delivery. The downward route for uncertain or flagged content enters a human-review system, shown here as Amazon A2I. A moderator inspects the image and its labels, then approves or rejects it. Approval returns to the delivery route; rejection blocks the image. The six numbered boxes below repeat these stages and emphasize that moderation occurs before delivery, not necessarily before generation. A2I is a historical option closed to new customers, so use the architecture to understand the human decision point rather than assuming new A2I access. The model outputs moderation labels; the application and reviewers apply policy.
